w: Founded c.679 by Osric, King of the Hwicce, rebuilt from 1089 by Abbot Serlo after a fire. William the Conqueror held his Christmas Court here in 1085, ordering the Domesday Book; Henry III was crowned here in 1216. The 14th-century cloisters hold the earliest fan vaulting, and the shrine of Edward II.
s: Where a king was crowned and fan vaulting was born
_facts: Founded c.679 by Osric, King of the Hwicce
William the Conqueror held Christmas Court here in 1085, ordering the Domesday Book
Henry III crowned here in 1216
Earliest surviving structural fan vaulting, 14th century

w: A former Benedictine monastery, now a parish church, with by repute the largest Romanesque crossing tower in England. Worship dates here to the 7th century; the abbey failed as a Wars of the Roses sanctuary. George Gilbert Scott restored it in the 19th century, and twelve bells still hang for change ringing.
s: England's grandest Romanesque tower, a failed sanctuary
_facts: Probably the largest, finest Romanesque crossing tower in England
Worship on site since the 7th century, priory founded 10th century
Failed as a sanctuary during the Wars of the Roses
Restored by George Gilbert Scott, 19th century

w: Before Gloucester, there was Glevum: a Roman fort refounded in AD 97 as a colonia for retired legionaries, formally Colonia Nervia Glevensium. The name never really left -- it survives on business signage across the city and in the Glevum Way, a 26-mile footpath looping the modern town.
s: The Roman colonia buried under modern Gloucester
_facts: Roman fort, refounded AD 97 as a colonia for retired legionaries
Formal name Colonia Nervia Glevensium
Name survives in the 26-mile Glevum Way footpath

w: Founded late 880s by Aethelflaed, daughter of Alfred the Great, and her husband Aethelred of Mercia, built as a near-copy of the Old Minster at Winchester. It anchored the Anglo-Saxon burh of Gloucester, but declined into a minor priory, suppressed in 1536, then wrecked in the Civil War. The ruins are Grade I listed.
s: A Saxon princess's priory, ruined since the Civil War
_facts: Founded late 880s/890s by Aethelflaed, daughter of Alfred the Great
Built as a copy of the Old Minster, Winchester
Suppressed 1536, largely demolished by 1643
Ruins are Grade I listed

w: A historic church on Westgate Street whose truncated spire has long served as a city-centre landmark. It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a Grade I listed building, and is now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust rather than by an active parish.
s: Westgate Street's spire, cut short but unmissable
_facts: Grade I listed, on Westgate Street
Truncated spire is a city-centre landmark
Cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust

w: Built soon after the Norman invasion and rebuilt in stone in the 12th or 13th century. Its owner, John Giffard, 2nd Lord of Brimpsfield, rebelled against Edward II and was executed in 1322 -- the castle was slighted in response. What remains: a mound with an outer bank and ditch, and a buried gatehouse.
s: A rebel lord's castle, slighted after his execution
_facts: Rebuilt in stone in the 12th or 13th century
Owner John Giffard rebelled against Edward II, executed 1322
Castle slighted afterward
Remains: mound, bank, ditch, gatehouse foundations

w: Thomas Telford's 150-foot stone arch, built 1825-28 to carry the road over the Severn's West Channel, sagged 2 inches when its centring was struck. Its profile is elliptical, segmental at the faces, a shape masons call corne de vache, cow's horn. Carried traffic until 1974, now a pedestrian-only scheduled monument.
s: Telford's cow's-horn arch over the Severn
_facts: Built by Thomas Telford, 1825-1828
150-foot arch span, based on a 1774 Paris design
Profile known as corne de vache, cow's horn
Now a pedestrian-only scheduled monument

w: Gloucester Abbey's monks drew water from springs on this hill in the 13th century; the city built reservoirs here in 1837-8 and drew supply until 1924, using them for storage until 1946 before backfilling the basins into car parks. The 650-foot summit is now a country park with a ski slope and golf course.
s: The hill that watered Gloucester for a century
_facts: Springs used by Gloucester Abbey in the 13th century
City reservoirs built 1837-8, water supply until 1924
650-foot summit, now a country park
Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust head office on site
